Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the exact click paths for installing Google Analytics 4 via Google Tag Manager, explicitly explaining how to build exploration funnels and customize acquisition reports to track campaign traffic. modules: [MEA] topics: [event contracts] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. event contracts / Differentiating between "Events" (any tracked interaction like scrolling or viewing a page) and "Key Events" (conversions). Creating a specific Key Event for a Thank You page by going to Admin > Events > Create Event, setting the parameter page_view, and matching the URL condition to thank-you. Using Google Tag Manager to deploy the GA4 Configuration tag by defining a constant variable for the Measurement ID and firing it on "Initialization - All Pages." Building Exploration Funnels / Using the "Explore" tab to create custom "Funnel Explorations" using e-commerce events (begin_checkout, add_payment_info, purchase). Explaining the difference between an "indirectly followed by" step (where users can view other pages in between) and a "directly followed by" step. Using "Path Explorations" to map user journeys. Adjusting GA4 Settings / Extending the data retention period from the default 2 months to 14 months to allow for historical lookbacks in Exploration reports. Enabling Google Signals to collect demographic data (age, gender, interests) and filtering out internal employee traffic via IP address configurations.

Look for. The specific regex string required to filter out default/non-campaign traffic in the Free Form Exploration report: ^\(.*\)$ (used with "Does Not Match Regex" to remove rows like "(organic)", "(direct)", and "(not set)"). The distinction between "User Acquisition" reports (which attribute based on the very first traffic source) and "Traffic Acquisition" reports (which attribute based on the most recent session). The specific click path to find the Measurement ID: Admin > Data Collection and Modification > Data Streams. The explanation of the "Platform" dimension (differentiating between Web and App data streams).

Skip. Basic explanations of what a timezone or currency setting is. The demonstration of the Gemini-powered "Analytics Advisor" AI chat feature, as it is a generic query interface. Plugs for the creator's "Google Analytics Glossary" or paid courses.

This is a complete walkthrough of Google Analytics. I'll show you how to set it up, how to use the reports, and how to track key events. I'll also cover newer features like built-in insights and 'Analytics Advisor', and share practical tips along the way to help you better understand your reports. We're going to start by creating a new Google Analytics account and property. If you're already using Google Analytics, you can log into your account and follow along. Okay, let's jump in and get started. We're looking at the Google Analytics product page on the Google Marketing Platform site. You can find it by navigating to 'marketing platform', 'dot', 'google', 'dot', 'com'. I've also included a link in the description below this video. This is where you can sign up for Google Analytics, and on the top right corner, we can see there are two options. If you already have a Google Analytics account, then you can sign in. So you can click this option to then access your existing Google Analytics account. Or if you're just getting started for the first time, then we can click 'Get Started Today' to create your account. Since I already have a Google Analytics account, I'm going to select 'Sign In To Analytics'. Now we need to login using our Google account. This can be your Gmail address, your Google Workspace address, or the login details you use to access other Google products. Since I already have an account, we can see we're looking at the reports. If you are getting started for the first time, then you won't see these reports, you will immediately be prompted to create a new Google Analytics account. To see this, let's navigate to 'Admin'. Then we click 'Create' at the top. And select 'Account'. This is what you will see if you selected 'Get Started Today' and you are creating your first Google Analytics account. To begin, we need to name our new account. The best way to think about a Google Analytics account is that it's used to organize things. Most businesses will have one account, and inside that account you'll create one or more properties. A property is where your data actually lives. It's what collects data from your website or app and turns it into reports. In most cases, you'll create one property for your business. That property can collect data from a single website, or from multiple websites and apps. So accounts organize properties, and properties collect and report on your data. Typically, you will want to name your account after your business. So I'm going to name my account 'Loves Data', but you can name your account anything you like. And if you need to set up Google Analytics for another business, you would create another account. So each business will have its own account. Below the account name, we have the data sharing options. These let you control how your data is shared. I recommend taking a moment to review these options. I'm going to leave the defaults. When you're happy, click 'Next'. Now that we've named our account, the next step is to create a property. I recommend naming the property so that it reflects the website, app, or combination of websites and apps you will be measuring. Since I'm just planning on measuring my website, I'm going to give the property the same name as my account. I'm going to name it 'Loves Data'. You can always change this if you need to. Next, we need to select the time zone we want to use for our reports. I suggest taking a bit of extra care at this stage, because if you decide to change the reporting time zone in the future, you will see a gap or overlap in data. I'm based in Sydney. So I'm going to select 'Australia'. And then 'Sydney' for my reporting time zone. Then we need to select the currency we want to use for our reports. I'm going to leave the currency set to 'US Dollars' for my property, but I suggest selecting the primary currency you use for your business or organization. I also want to highlight that the currency you select can be used for automatic currency conversion in your reports. For example, if I send a value in Australian Dollars to Google Analytics and I have US Dollars selected, then the Australian Dollar amounts will be automatically converted to US dollars. Once you're happy with the details for your property, click 'Next'. Now we need to tell Google about our business. We need to select an industry category. And the size of our business. And let's click 'Next'. We're now asked to choose our business objectives. The selections we make here control which pre-configured reports will be added to our property. I recommend selecting the 'Other Business Objectives' option as this will give you a full set of reports and basically includes everything that's available in the other four options. So let's select 'Other Business Objectives'. And then click 'Create'. We need to agree to the terms of service for our particular country. I'm going to select 'Australia'. And accept the terms. We have now created our new Google Analytics account and property. And we can see the next step is to choose a platform. This is where you are going to install Google Analytics and the selection we make here will create a data stream. A data stream is used to collect data into your property and reports. You can create one data stream, or multiple data streams. For example, if you're going to be measuring a single website, then you will just have one. But if you want to measure a website and an app, you will have two data streams. So just remember, a data stream is used to send data to Google Analytics, and the data will then be processed into your reports. We can choose the type of stream we want to create. Since I'm going to be measuring my website, I'm going to select 'Web'. Now we can enter the URL of our website and name the stream. For my stream, I'm going to enter 'www', 'dot', 'loves data', 'dash', 'test', 'dot', 'com' as the URL. And I'm going to name the stream 'Loves Data Website'. Next, we can adjust the enhanced measurement settings. Enhanced measurement lets you automatically track a range of actions on your website without needing to add or adjust any code. It will automatically track page views, plus people scrolling pages on your website, clicks on outbound links, and your website's search function. It will also track forms, people watching embedded YouTube videos, and people downloading files. Enhanced measurement is enabled by default and it's a great starting point, but it's worth reviewing these events to make sure they align with what you actually want to measure on your website. You also have the option of disabling the events that are automatically collected by enhanced measurement. To do this, you can click the configuration icon. And then disable (or enable) the actions you want to automatically track. For example, if you don't want to report on people engaging with forms on your website, you can disable this option. And then click 'Save'. Then when you're happy, click the button to create your data stream. Our data stream has now been created. And after we wait a moment, we can see installation instructions are loaded. Google Analytics will try to automatically identify the platform used for your website. You can use these to install Google Analytics. Or you can view additional options. For example, you can select the option to choose your CMS to be guided through the installation steps. Let's close this. Details are now loaded for our data stream. Apart from using the installation instructions, you can also copy the measurement ID on the top right corner. When we add this on our website, using either the Google Tag or Google Tag Manager, measurement ID ensures that data flows into our property and our reports. In most cases, I recommend using Google Tag Manager instead of the Google Tag because it provides added flexibility. You can manage multiple tags, not just Google Analytics using Google Tag Manager, and you can also configure Google Tag Manager to track a whole range of other actions and elements on your website. Now that we've covered the steps to create a new account and property, we're going to start exploring our reports. Then, later in this video, we will look at installing Google Analytics and important configuration options. To explore the reports, we're going to use Google's demo account. This lets you follow along and explore real data, even if you haven't set up your own property yet. To access the demo account, let's head to my blog. I've included a link to this in the description below this video. Let's click the link to access the demo property for the Google Merchandise Store. We're now looking at Google's demo property. This is the perfect way to explore Google Analytics and experiment with the reports you can customize. This property shows us data from Google's merchandise store, which sells a range of Google branded products, like t-shirts, hats and other accessories. At the top, we can select the drop-down to quickly switch between the different accounts and properties we have access to in Google Analytics. This is useful if you're looking after Google Analytics for multiple businesses. We're going to stick with Google's demo. On the left, we have the main menu that lets us navigate between the different types of reports in Google Analytics. First is 'Home'. This provides a top-level summary for your website. At the top we can see automated insights based on Google's AI. These insights are different for each property, and they highlight unusual changes or trends that Google Analytics thinks are worth looking at. Below these AI-driven insights, we can see top-level summaries from our reports. Using the menu, we can see 'Reports', which is where you can find the pre-configured reports. This includes dedicated reports showing you how people find your website, what pages they've viewed, if they've converted, plus demographics and details about the devices they're using. 'Explore' lets you create custom reports, and you can visualize data in different ways. For example, you can create simple tables, funnel visualizations, and more. A helpful way to think about this is that 'Reports' are best for monitoring what's happening on your website, while Explore is best when you have a specific question you want to answer. Next is 'Advertising', these reports show you the relationship between your different marketing channels and how they lead to conversions on your website. And finally, on the bottom left corner is 'Admin'. This lets us access additional settings for our account and property. Before we look at some of the most important reports, it's worth knowing that Google Analytics offers a lot of different ways to view your data. This includes pre-configured reports and custom exploration reports you can build yourself. The goal isn't to learn every report. It's to understand the reports that help you make sense of what's happening on your website. Okay, so we're still looking at the home report. And below the AI-driven insights, we can see the total number of active users and the total number of key events. Key events are used to report on conversions, so any action that is important for your business. We can also see the number of sessions, so the number of times people have visited the website. And we can also see the total number of purchases. These totals are for the last 14 days, but we can change this by clicking the current selection. And choosing a new one. Now we can see all the metrics are updated. We can also see a trendline for the metric that is currently selected. This is showing us our user trend. And the dotted line shows us a comparison to the previous period, which is the same number of days before our currently selected date range. In the next card, we can see the total number of active users that have been on our website in the last 30 minutes. Below this we can see any reports and settings we've recently viewed. And at the bottom we can see any insights and recommendations. These can include automated insights which are based on Google's AI. These insights are designed to help you quickly spot unexpected changes in your data. You also have the option of configuring custom insights based on metrics and conditions you choose. Now let's navigate to 'Reports'. We're now looking at the 'Reports Snapshot' which is similar to the home report we just looked at. We can see the number of active users, new users, average engagement time, and event count. Below these metrics, we can see the top pages people have viewed on the website. This includes the number of 'Views', so 'Page Views', the number of 'Active Users', the total number of events collected on each page and the bounce rate. Traveling down further, we can see more cards. We can see the top ways new users are finding us. We can see the top traffic sources that are driving sessions. The trend for new and returning users. And more. Since Google Analytics includes a lot of different terminology, I want to quickly mention a handy resource I've created for you. It's my Google Analytics Glossary. If you're just getting started, this can really help as new terms come up. I've included a link in the description below this video. Now let's navigate to the 'Realtime Overview' report. This report lets you view details about the people who are currently on your website. Data is processed into the reports within a few seconds. This can be useful for identifying where people are landing on your website. For example, if you're sending out an important email campaign, then you can check that people are viewing the pages you expect as they click through to your website. And each card includes a bar chart. This is read from right to left, so the current minute is on the right, and then each bar stepping to the left represents another minute contained in the last 30 minutes. We can also see the total number of active users on the website in the last 30 minutes, and the last 5 minutes. The geographic map shows us where people are located. Apart from the overview report, there's also a dedicated 'Realtime Pages' report. Let's open this report. This report just focuses on the pages people are currently viewing on your website. You can travel through the table using the arrows on the right, and you can narrow down on pages using the search option on the left. Now let's select 'Acquisition'. And then 'Overview'. The acquisition reports are all about how people are finding the website. On the overview report we can see similar details that we saw on the home report and the reports snapshot. We can see the number of active users and new users. And again, we have the realtime card on the right. Traveling down, we can then see how new users are finding the website. You can also use the links at the bottom of the cards to view the full report. And we can also adjust the date range used for the report. Let's select the current date range. This lets you send custom information about how products are being grouped and displayed on your website. You can also track items being purchased based on promotions you are offering. This means you haven't enabled Google Signals yet. We will talk about Google Signals in a moment, but for your property, once you've enabled the feature you will be able to see these additional details for your users. Again, like the other reports we've seen, selecting 'Country' lets us change the report. For example, we can choose 'City'. To see the metrics broken-down by city. And you might be wondering about 'not set'. This is telling us that there are a portion of users where the city is unknown. Basically, Google Analytics has collected details about the user, but isn't able to provide this specific information we've asked for in the report. So you can think of 'not set' as 'unknown' in Google Analytics. Now let's select 'Tech'. And then 'Overview'. Since this property only has a web data stream, we can see one hundred percent of users are associated with the 'Web' platform. If you have editor or administrator access, you'll also see a 'Library' option at the bottom of the reporting menu. This lets you customize the menu and the reports. We're going to walk through the steps to create two exploration reports. First, I'll show you how to create a report that highlights the custom campaigns sending people to your website. For example, you can create a funnel based on page views to see how people travel through particular pages on your website. Okay, let's name the first step 'Begin Checkout'. These reports help you understand how your marketing channels work together and how they contribute to conversions. Let's navigate to 'Advertising'. These reports are useful once you've linked Google Analytics to Google Ads and you're tracking key events. Basically, 'Key Events' are used to report on important actions in Google Analytics. While 'Conversions' are used in Google Ads. While Google Ads uses 'Conversions' for reporting and optimization.
